summary: Initial discovery to understand Lynx Energy's inference cost constraints and hosting preferences. Key drivers: tight monthly budget cap, 200ms SLO on customer-facing flows, desire for private VPC or hybrid model due to PII in prompts. Evaluated Hosted, Dedicated, and Private tradeoffs; discussed batching and KV/prefix caching levers, reserved commit economics, and quick pilot to measure token costs.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private economics
Next steps: pricing worksheet and benchmark pilot
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Hey everyone thanks for carving out the time. Jordan from Redwood inference, AE on this account. Maya from our solutions engineering team is with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Carlos (Lynx): Good, thanks. Running tight but excited to dig in.
[00:12] Maya (Redwood): Hi all. We'll try to focus on the practical tradeoffs — unit cost, latency, and what hosting modes look like for Lynx.
[00:18] Priya (Lynx): Quick context: we're building a customer support assistant that reads meter telemetry and customer notes. Prompts may contain PII and sometimes small file excerpts. We're constrained on budget — roughly $25k/mo for inference for the first 6 months.
[00:30] Noah (Lynx): Our traffic profile: peak 220 req/s, steady 80 req/s, avg token output around 120 tokens per response. P95 latency needs to stay under 200ms for the live chat flow, otherwise CS gets upset.
[00:44] Jordan: Great that's helpful. Quick callouts: Hosted API gives fastest onboarding and per-token pricing, Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and lower per-token cost at scale, Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you network isolation and control for PII but has higher ops overhead and usually an upfront platform fee.
[01:05] Carlos: We're trying to decide whether we can start hosted and move to dedicated or private later. The main fear is the bill spiking and not being able to hit our $25k budget.
[01:14] Maya: Totally fair. Two levers we use to control unit cost: batching and prefix/KV caching. Batching lowers per-token GPU overhead by amortizing kernel launch and memory movement across requests; effective for predictably short latencies and when you have throughput headroom. KV/prefix cache avoids recomputing initial context for repeated prompt patterns — big wins for chatty or templated prompts.
[01:30] Priya: How big of a win is caching? Our flows often repeat customer metadata and meter templates.
[01:35] Maya: In our benchmarks, for templated prompts with stable prefixes, you can reduce token compute up to 30-60% depending on cache hit rate and model architecture. So if your average tokens are 120 and 40% of requests hit the cache you can see material cost reductions.
[01:50] Carlos: What about batching — doesn't that increase latency? We care about p95.
[01:55] Maya: There's a trade. Continuous batching (small micro-batches sub-10ms queuing) plus latency SLO-aware routing can keep p95 within your target if your baseline service is under 150ms. We can configure a latency-first policy that routes lower-priority traffic to larger batch sizes and keeps critical chat on low-latency paths.
[02:12] Priya: We're worried about tail spikes during morning high load. Is dedicated better for that?
[02:16] Jordan: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity so you have headroom and predictable token throughput. You also get a lower committed price per token because you buy the capacity; but you pay even when not fully utilized. There's also burst options.
[02:29] Noah: On the budget math, do you have a simple model of hosted per-token vs dedicated effective cost if we commit to X GPUs?
[02:36] Jordan: Yes — we'll send a pricing worksheet. Quick thumb: hosted per-token for text gen is Xc/token at small scale (Jordan mumble: our published rates) but at our Dedicated tiers, effective cost can drop 30-50% depending on utilization and model quantization.
[02:50] Priya: You just said quantization — we run smaller models (7B-13B) mostly; do those help?
[02:56] Maya: Absolutely. Quantized models reduce memory bandwidth and can increase throughput per GPU. If you can accept slight quality delta, 4-bit or mixed precision can drastically lower per-token cost on dedicated or private deployments.
[03:08] Carlos: Security and compliance — we need SOC2 + KMS integration and SAML SSO for the console. Any blockers?
[03:15] Jordan: Hosted supports SOC2, KMS integrations for customer key wrapping, and SSO. For PII-sensitive flows customers often go Dedicated or Private to control key material and network. For Private we can support customer-managed KMS/HSM and air-gapped installs but that adds setup time.
[03:29] Noah: How long does private deployment take? We have regulatory windows.
[03:33] Maya: Typical Private with VPC control plane is 6-8 weeks; on-prem air-gapped can be longer and we’ll need an infra runbook. Dedicated is faster — usually 2-4 weeks depending on GPU provision. Hosted is immediate (hours to days).
[03:47] Priya: One other concern: model fallbacks — if capacity is constrained we don't want failed requests.
[03:51] Jordan: Our smart routing can fall back to compatible model variants in another region or to a smaller model. You can configure SLO-aware fallback chains. We'll show example policies in the deep-dive.
[04:02] Carlos: Pricing examples would help. Could you show a scenario where we keep within $25k/mo?
[04:07] Jordan: Sure. Rough example: assume 5M tokens/mo (back of envelope). Hosted might cost $A (Jordan says: approx $0.02/token at small tiers — verbatim gets fuzzy), Dedicated with 1x reserved pool at 60% utilization might be less than half that. The real lever is utilization and caching.
[04:25] Noah: Let's be concrete — our math: 80 req/s steady * 120 tokens * 30 days * 3600 = roughly 25.9M tokens/mo. Oops that's much higher than I first said.
[04:40] Priya: Right we mis-communicated; peak doesn't mean steady. If we assume 6 hours peak and rest low, maybe total 7M tokens/mo.
[04:49] Maya: That changes the calculus. At low sustained usage hosted can be easiest and safe for budget if you use caching and rate-limiting. For predictable 7M tokens/mo, a small dedicated commit could be cost-effective if you expect growth to 20-30M tokens/mo.
[05:02] Jordan: On burst protection, our Dedicated customers can configure burst credits — pay-as-you-go above commit. That smooths spikes without over-committing.
[05:11] Carlos: Are there any hard limits on model size or sequence length in Dedicated or Private?
[05:16] Maya: Not hard limits, but larger sequence lengths impact memory and batching. Our runtime picks kernels and splits KV caches to optimize. We'll want specifics on average context length and checkpoint.
[05:27] Priya: Noah will send sample traces.
[05:30] (brief cross-talk)
[05:33] Jordan: A few pragmatic recommendations for your team: 1) Start hosted, enable prefix/KV cache for templated bits, 2) Use latency-first routing for chat flow and route lower priority inference to batched endpoints, 3) After a month of telemetry if tokens >~12M/mo consider a small Dedicated commit to lower unit cost.
[05:52] Carlos: Sounds reasonable. What's the best way to test cost differences quickly?
[05:55] Maya: We can run a 2-week pilot where we replay a small sample of your traffic against hosted and a dedicated reserved pool with the same model and measure token spend, p95 latency, and cache hit rate. That gives reliable unit-econ comparisons.
[06:10] Priya: We want to ensure the pilot includes KV cache enabled and a quantized model variant to see the full savings.
[06:16] Maya: Yes we'll include both. Also will include tooling to estimate amortized cost per token with your traffic profile.
[06:23] Noah: One ops question: if we go with Private VPC, how do software upgrades and fallback work?
[06:27] Jordan: For VPC Private we provide a control plane with canary rollouts — you can opt-in for automatic upgrades or manual. Fallbacks are same as hosted if you permit outbound to Redwood control plane; fully air-gapped on-prem will have different mechanics and slower updates.
[06:40] Carlos: Any immediate compliance red flags?
[06:43] Maya: None from what you described — SOC2 + KMS + SSO are supported. For regulated data we recommend Private with customer-managed KMS or using tokenization/PII redaction in the prompt layer.
[06:56] Jordan: Okay let's recap next steps: we'll send the pricing worksheet and a sample unit-econ model. Maya will propose a technical deep dive and pilot plan. Noah will send traffic traces and sample prompts. You'll review security contacts for Private.
[07:14] Priya: Sounds good. Also can you include examples of batching config and the tradeoff numbers?
[07:19] Maya: Yes, the runbook includes micro-batching latencies, recommended max queue ms for p95 targets, and configuration examples for cross-request KV cache TTLs.
[07:30] Carlos: Thanks everyone. We'll review and sync next week.
[07:34] Jordan: Thanks all. We'll follow up in email with attachments and scheduling options.
[07:38] (meeting ends)

Notes: transcript has some imperfect bits — e.g., some rate numbers were approximated, and Jordan referenced published rates which should be validated in the pricing worksheet. The team expressed a preference to start Hosted + caching then transition to Dedicated if utilization justifies commit.
questions: What monthly commit would make Dedicated cheaper than Hosted for our profile?
How quickly can Private be provisioned and what are the on-prem timelines?
Can you include quantization tradeoffs and expected quality delta for 7B models?
